questions.q: A nightly job runs custom C++ libraries inside a container for about 2 hours. The team wants no scheduler servers to manage. Which service fits best?

options.why: Wrong: Lambda stops at 15 minutes.
Wrong: Glue is for Spark ETL on catalog data and may not fit custom native dependencies.

options.t: AWS Batch with a container image
options.why: Right: Batch runs long containerized jobs with queues, retries and scale to zero, and has no scheduler to run.
Wrong: you would manage the server, scaling and failures yourself.

questions.explain: Batch is the managed answer for long, custom, containerized compute jobs.
questions.remember: Long (over 15 min), custom-container, any-language jobs with queuing and retries → AWS Batch. Spark/catalog ETL → Glue.
variants: Short event-driven task under 15 minutes → Lambda.
Spark or SQL ETL on data-lake tables with least ops → Glue.
Distributed Spark/Hive cluster → EMR.

questions.q: A company must apply the same transformation to 8,000 S3 files with one submission. Each task must know which file to process. What should they use?

options.t: One array job of size 8,000 using `AWS_BATCH_JOB_ARRAY_INDEX` to pick the file
options.why: Right: one SubmitJob creates the child jobs and each child reads its own index.
Wrong: SubmitJob is limited to 50 TPS per account, so this is slow and clumsy.
Wrong: MNP is for tightly coupled jobs like MPI, not independent files.
Wrong: dependsOn allows at most 20 dependencies.

questions.explain: Array jobs fan out thousands of independent children from one submit.
questions.remember: Many independent items, same code → array job (size 2-10,000); the child uses AWS_BATCH_JOB_ARRAY_INDEX to choose its input.
variants: 20,000 files → array size is capped at 10,000, so submit two arrays or batch files per child.
Tightly coupled MPI across nodes → multi-node parallel job.
Child i must wait for child i of another array → N_TO_N dependency.

questions.q: Fault-tolerant file conversion jobs must run at the lowest cost and the account should pay nothing when no jobs are queued. Which compute environment settings fit?

options.why: Wrong: warm instances cost money all day and On-Demand is dearer.
Right: Spot is cheaper, and minvCpus 0 scales the environment to zero when the queue is empty.
Wrong: you manage the instances yourself and they do not scale to zero.
Wrong: maxvCpus 0 would allow no jobs to run at all.

questions.explain: Spot plus minvCpus 0 is the classic cheapest Batch setup.
questions.remember: Cheapest Batch: Spot (with retries) and minvCpus = 0. maxvCpus is the spending ceiling, minvCpus above 0 keeps instances warm and billed.
variants: Jobs must start instantly every morning → keep minvCpus above 0 during working hours.
Need to cap total spend → lower maxvCpus.
Small spiky jobs with no instance management → Fargate or Fargate Spot.

questions.q: Jobs on a Spot CE sometimes fail with the status reason `Host EC2 (instance i-0abc) terminated`. Application errors should not be retried. What is the best fix?

options.why: Wrong: 1 is the default and means no retry.
Wrong: the allocation strategy does not stop Spot interruptions and BEST_FIT can limit scaling.
Wrong: this is not a timeout problem.

options.t: A retry strategy with `evaluateOnExit` matching `onStatusReason: Host EC2*` to RETRY and a catch-all EXIT
options.why: Right: retries only host-level interruptions and exits on real application errors.

questions.explain: Retry on Host EC2* to survive Spot interruptions.
questions.remember: Spot interruption shows as 'Host EC2 ... terminated'. Use attempts (1-10) with evaluateOnExit matching Host EC2* → RETRY, else EXIT, plus checkpointing.
variants: Container killed for memory (exit 137) → raise the MEMORY request, retrying will not help.
Cancelled or terminated jobs → never retried.
Long Spot job restarting from zero → add checkpointing to S3 or DynamoDB.

questions.q: A Batch EC2 Spot environment often has to wait because the preferred instance type is unavailable. Which allocation strategy is AWS's recommended choice for Spot?

options.why: Right: it weighs price and interruption risk across many pools and is recommended for most Spot use.
Wrong: it is the default, waits for one best type and can limit scaling.
Wrong: this one is for On-Demand and follows your ordering.
Wrong: recommended for On-Demand, not the Spot recommendation.

questions.explain: Use SPOT_PRICE_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED for Spot, BEST_FIT_PROGRESSIVE for On-Demand.
questions.remember: Spot → SPOT_PRICE_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED (price + interruption risk). On-Demand → BEST_FIT_PROGRESSIVE. BEST_FIT is the default but can stall scaling.
variants: Spot pools least likely to be interrupted regardless of price → SPOT_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED.
On-Demand following your own type order → BEST_FIT_PROGRESSIVE_ORDERED.
Fargate or ECS Managed Instances CE → no allocation strategy applies.

questions.q: A job requests 16 GiB memory on a CE whose only instance type has exactly 16 GiB. The job stays in RUNNABLE forever. What is the cause?

options.t: The job is in STARTING because of an image pull
options.why: Wrong: STARTING is a different state, and the job here was never placed.

options.t: The queue is FIFO and must be switched to fair-share
options.why: Wrong: scheduling order does not change whether a job fits.

options.t: The ECS agent and OS reserve memory, so the job never fits; request a bit less
options.why: Right: usable memory is below the instance total, so a full-size request cannot be placed.

options.t: Batch does not allow more than 10 GiB per job
options.why: Wrong: no such limit; large memory is a reason to choose Batch.

questions.explain: Ask for slightly less than the instance memory.
questions.remember: RUNNABLE forever = no CE can fit it: over-large request (including all of an instance's memory), maxvCpus or vCPU quota hit, INVALID CE, or network registration failure.
variants: Job exceeded its memory while running → killed (OOM, exit 137) and FAILED.
maxvCpus reached → RUNNABLE until capacity frees up.
One bad job blocking the head → jobStateTimeLimitActions to cancel stuck RUNNABLE jobs.

questions.q: Three teams share one Batch queue and one team floods it, starving the others. What should the data engineer configure?

options.why: Wrong: more capacity does not change the FIFO order.

options.t: A fair-share scheduling policy with a share identifier per team
options.why: Right: fair-share divides capacity between share identifiers so one backlog cannot starve the rest.
Wrong: allocation picks instance types, not job order.

options.t: More than 3 CEs on the queue
options.why: Wrong: a queue holds at most 3 CEs and it would not change fairness.

questions.explain: Fair-share scheduling policy is the fairness tool.
questions.remember: Default queue order is FIFO. Shared teams → scheduling policy with share identifiers. Urgent vs backfill → a high-priority queue on the same CE.
variants: Urgent jobs behind backfill → separate queue with a higher priority sharing the CE.
Only 5 licenses exist → consumable resources.
Cap total spend → maxvCpus.

questions.q: A queue should use cheap Spot first and still finish jobs when Spot capacity runs out. What is the right design?

options.t: Two separate queues, one per CE, and manual resubmits
options.why: Wrong: adds manual work, the ordered CE list does this automatically.
Wrong: keeps instances warm but does not add a fallback.
Wrong: a queue allows at most 3 compute environments.

options.t: One queue listing the Spot CE first and an On-Demand CE second
options.why: Right: the queue tries its CEs in order, so On-Demand acts as overflow.

questions.explain: Order CEs in the queue: cheap first, reliable second.
questions.remember: A job queue has up to 3 CEs tried in order: Spot then On-Demand, or Fargate then EC2.
variants: Max CEs per queue → 3; max CEs per Region → 50; max queues per Region → 50.
A queue cannot be fixed by mixing Fargate with GPU needs → GPU needs an EC2 CE.
Batch on EKS → up to 5 Batch CEs per EKS cluster.

questions.q: An ETL workflow must run a Lambda extract, then a Batch transform that finishes before a Glue load step starts, with retries and error handling. What is the best way to run the Batch step?

options.why: Right: Step Functions submits the job and waits for it to succeed or fail, with no polling code.
Wrong: the state ends as soon as the job is submitted, so Glue would start too early.

options.t: A Lambda that sleeps and polls `DescribeJobs`
options.why: Wrong: Lambda is limited to 15 minutes and polling code is extra work.

options.t: EventBridge rule on a schedule only
options.why: Wrong: it starts a job but does not coordinate the next steps.

questions.explain: Use .sync to make Step Functions wait for the Batch job.
questions.remember: Orchestrate Batch with Step Functions batch:submitJob.sync (waits). Airflow users → MWAA BatchOperator. Simple chains → dependsOn.
variants: Team already uses Airflow → MWAA BatchOperator.
Plain submitJob without .sync → does not wait.
Simple extract → transform → load without an orchestrator → dependsOn (up to 20 jobs).

questions.q: A containerized aggregation must run every night at 02:00, and the team must be alerted if it fails. Which design is best?

options.t: A Lambda function with a 2-hour sleep
options.why: Wrong: Lambda stops at 15 minutes.

options.t: A scheduled EventBridge target calling Batch SubmitJob, plus an EventBridge rule on Batch Job State Change = FAILED to SNS
options.why: Right: schedule and failure alerting both use EventBridge, with SNS for notification.
Wrong: CloudTrail records API calls, not job failures.

options.t: A CE with `minvCpus` above 0 and no schedule
options.why: Wrong: warm instances do not start a job at 02:00.

questions.explain: Schedule through EventBridge, alert on Batch Job State Change.
questions.remember: Batch emits Job State Change events to EventBridge. Match FAILED → SNS or Lambda for alerts. EventBridge needs a role with batch:SubmitJob to start jobs.
variants: Each S3 upload must start a job → S3 to EventBridge to Batch target, passing the key as a parameter.
Queue head cannot run → Job queue blocked event.
Who submitted or changed a queue → CloudTrail.

questions.q: A Batch job's code must read one S3 prefix and write to DynamoDB, following least privilege. Which role should carry those permissions?

options.why: Wrong: shared by every job on the host, so permissions are too broad.
Wrong: it lets Batch manage EC2, ECS and Auto Scaling, not your code.

options.t: The job role (`jobRoleArn`) of the job definition
options.why: Right: the job role is what your container code assumes, and it is set per job definition.
Wrong: it pulls images, fetches secrets and writes logs, not your application's data access.

questions.explain: Data access for your code belongs on the job (task) role.
questions.remember: Service role = Batch manages infra. Instance role = ECS agent on EC2. Execution role = pull images, fetch secrets, logs (required for Fargate). Job role = your code's permissions.
variants: AccessDenied from S3 inside a job → job role missing or too narrow, or KMS/bucket policy denies.
Job fails to fetch a secret at start → execution role permissions.
Containers must not reach the instance role → IMDSv2 with hop limit 1.

questions.q: A job needs a database password at runtime. The password must not appear in the image, command or plain environment variables. What should be used?

options.why: Wrong: visible in the job definition in plain text.

options.t: An argument in `command` through a parameter
options.why: Wrong: parameters and commands are visible in job details.

options.t: Baking it into the ECR image
options.why: Wrong: anyone with the image can read it.

options.t: The `secrets` field in the job definition referencing Secrets Manager or Parameter Store
options.why: Right: values are injected as environment variables at start, and the execution role reads them.

questions.explain: Use `secrets` plus an execution role that can read them.
questions.remember: Secrets → job definition `secrets` (Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store); the execution role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue / ssm:GetParameters and kms:Decrypt if encrypted.
variants: Who needs the permission to fetch secrets → the execution role.
Fargate job fails with ResourceInitializationError → cannot fetch secrets or pull image (role or network).
Many jobs hitting RDS → limit parallelism, use RDS Proxy.

questions.q: Batch CEs run in private subnets with no NAT gateway. Jobs fail with `CannotPullContainerError`. Which fix gives access to ECR without NAT?

options.t: Interface endpoints for ECR API and DKR, an S3 gateway endpoint, and a CloudWatch Logs endpoint
options.why: Right: image layers are stored in S3, so ECR endpoints plus the S3 gateway endpoint cover the pull; logs need their own endpoint.
Wrong: pulls also need the DKR endpoint and S3, which holds the layers.

options.t: Move the CE to an unmanaged environment
options.why: Wrong: it does not change network paths.
Wrong: this is a network problem, not capacity.

questions.explain: Private subnets need NAT or VPC endpoints for ECR, S3 and logs.
questions.remember: No route to ECR/S3 → CannotPullContainerError. Add ecr.api, ecr.dkr, S3 gateway, logs (and ECS endpoints for EC2 CEs), or a NAT. Endpoints also save NAT per-GB cost.
variants: Docker Hub rate limits → ECR pull-through cache.
Fargate in a public subnet → needs assignPublicIp or NAT.
Wrong image URI/tag or missing ECR permission → same error.

questions.q: A team wants to find the stdout of a failed Batch job and stop log costs from growing forever. What is correct?

options.t: Logs go to S3 by default and expire after 30 days
options.why: Wrong: default is CloudWatch Logs and logs do not expire.

options.t: Logs go to `/aws/batch/job` by default, so find the stream via `DescribeJobs` and set a retention period on the log group
options.why: Right: the default group never expires logs, retention must be set.

options.t: Logs appear only in the ECS console
options.why: Wrong: the Batch job details link to CloudWatch Logs streams.
Wrong: CloudTrail records API calls, not container output.

questions.explain: Default group /aws/batch/job; retention is never set by default.
questions.remember: Container stdout/stderr → CloudWatch Logs group /aws/batch/job (stream jobDefinitionName/default/<task-id>); never expires by default, so set retention.
variants: Ship logs to OpenSearch or Splunk → awsfirelens or splunk log driver in the job definition.
Cluster CPU/memory → Container Insights.
First place to look for why a job failed → statusReason, container.reason and exitCode.

questions.q: An engineer wants an email whenever any Batch job ends in FAILED, without polling. What is the simplest solution?

options.t: A CloudWatch alarm on a native Batch FailedJobs metric
options.why: Wrong: not a built-in metric path in the notes; job counts are usually built from events.
Wrong: polling is wasteful when events exist.

options.t: An EventBridge rule on Batch Job State Change with status FAILED, targeting an SNS topic
options.why: Right: Batch emits state-change events carrying status reason and exit code.
Wrong: audits API activity, not job outcomes.

questions.explain: Batch Job State Change event → SNS.
questions.remember: Job status alerts come from EventBridge events (Job State Change, queue blocked) routed to SNS, Lambda or Step Functions.
variants: Auto-resubmit failed jobs → route the event to Lambda.
Job queue head cannot run → Job queue blocked event.
Who submitted the job → CloudTrail.

questions.q: Jobs in a Batch EC2 environment start slowly every morning after the CE scaled to zero overnight, and the images are large. Which changes improve start time? (Choose two.)

options.why: Right: warm instances avoid the minutes spent launching EC2.
Wrong: that prevents jobs from running.
Right: image pull time shows in STARTING, so smaller images start sooner.
Wrong: this does not affect launch or pull time.
Wrong: retries do not speed up the first start.

questions.explain: Two delays: instance launch and image pull.
questions.remember: Start time = EC2 launch from zero + image pull (shown in STARTING). Fix with minvCpus > 0, smaller images, ECR in-Region, pull-through cache, custom AMI, or Fargate for small jobs.
variants: Small, short jobs without instance management → Fargate.
Large dependencies → pre-bake into a custom AMI.
Cost trade-off: minvCpus above 0 is billed even when idle, so set it back to 0 if warm starts are not needed.

questions.q: A job must run on a GPU with large local storage. Which compute environment type should be chosen?

options.why: Wrong: Fargate does not support the GPU jobs described in the notes.
Wrong: same limitation, and it can be interrupted.

options.t: An EC2 compute environment with GPU instance types and `GPU` in `resourceRequirements`
options.why: Right: GPU jobs need EC2 instance types, not Fargate.

options.t: An unmanaged CE with no instances
options.why: Wrong: no capacity would exist to run jobs.

questions.explain: GPU, multi-node, big memory, custom AMIs, privileged containers → EC2 CE.
questions.remember: Fargate: small/medium jobs, isolation, no instance management, needs an execution role. EC2: GPU, multi-node parallel, huge memory/vCPU, custom AMI, privileged.
variants: A 32-node MPI job → multi-node parallel on EC2 with EFA and a cluster placement group.
Many small spiky jobs → Fargate.
Fargate job pulling from ECR → needs the execution role.

questions.q: A company needs 3,000 CSV files converted to Parquet with custom code at the lowest cost. Retries and duplicate rows are a concern. What is the best design?

options.why: Wrong: slow and more expensive.

options.t: An array job on a Spot CE with retries on host termination and idempotent writes to deterministic S3 keys
options.why: Right: array jobs fan out cheaply, Spot cuts cost, and idempotent outputs make retries safe.

options.t: A single job on Fargate looping over all files
options.why: Wrong: no parallelism and a failure restarts everything.

options.t: A Glue Spark job reading CSVs
options.why: Wrong: fits plain Spark on catalog tables, but the scenario calls for custom code at lowest cost with Batch.

questions.remember: Jobs can be retried, so write to deterministic keys or temp prefixes and commit; checkpoint long jobs. Chunk tiny files so container start is amortized.
variants: Plain Spark on catalog tables with least ops → Glue, not Batch.
A final merge step after the array → job with dependsOn the array.
Tiny jobs wasting start time → group several files per child.
